title: How Children Pick Up Their First Language
brief: Explain in plain English how first language (L1) acquisition works: children absorb language from their environment through listening, interaction, and meaningful exposure before they can produce it. Draw on the module's description of Total Physical Response—where learners first respond with actions only and only later begin producing language—as a concrete illustration of the listen-before-speak pattern seen in L1 development. Use the module's notes on very young learners (short attention spans, need for realia and actions to make input comprehensible) to show that meaning must be understood before language sticks. Keep jargon-free; no deep SLA theory here.

title: What Changes When You Learn a Second Language
brief: Contrast L1 acquisition with second language (L2) learning by drawing on source material about adult and mixed-level classroom contexts, including the bilingual classroom setting described in the module (English and Spanish). Highlight that L2 learners already have a fully formed first language and a developed mind, which shapes how they approach new input—they can use reasoning, inference, and prior knowledge in ways infants cannot. Use the module's references to integrated language skills, contextualization, and linking language to real communicative situations to show that L2 learning benefits from purposeful, meaningful exposure rather than rote repetition. Avoid deep SLA terminology; keep the tone accessible.

title: Comprehensible Input: The Core Idea
brief: Introduce the concept of comprehensible input in plain English: language that learners can mostly understand, with meaning supported by context, actions, visuals, and realia. Draw directly on the module's examples—using realia and actions to make vocabulary comprehensible to young learners, Total Physical Response, songs with movement, concept-checking questions, and graphic organizers—to show what comprehensible input looks like in practice. Explain that when learners understand the message, language acquisition can happen naturally alongside content learning. This section should feel practical and grounded in classroom observation, not theoretical.

title: Krashen's Input Hypothesis: Influential but Not Settled Science
brief: Give a brief, honest account of Stephen Krashen's Input Hypothesis—the idea that learners acquire language when they receive input just beyond their current level—presenting it as historically important and widely discussed, not as proven fact. Cite Gregg (1984) to make the honest caveat clear: while comprehensible input clearly matters in classroom practice (as the module's examples confirm), the strong version of Krashen's hypothesis is not empirically testable as stated, meaning teachers should treat it as a useful orienting idea rather than settled science. Keep the tone balanced and reassuring—theory informs practice but does not dictate it. No additional SLA frameworks should be introduced here.

title: The Learner's Own Language: English-Mainly, Not English-Only
brief: Address the common assumption that good language classrooms must be English-only, and explain why the field has moved away from this position. Anchor the discussion in the module's classroom example where the teacher allows judicious use of the shared first language (L1) at specific moments in the lesson, and cite Hall & Cook (2012) to confirm that research supports a shift toward 'English-mainly' rather than a strict monolingual rule. Explain that the learner's L1 can be a resource—for checking understanding, clarifying meaning, and reducing anxiety—when used thoughtfully. Reassure trainee teachers that allowing some L1 use is professionally defensible and learner-centred.

title: What This Means for Your Classroom
brief: Bring the unit together with practical takeaways: prioritise making input comprehensible through context, visuals, movement, and concept-checking questions (all drawn from the module); treat Krashen's ideas as a helpful lens rather than a rulebook (Gregg, 1984); and feel confident using the learners' L1 judiciously rather than banning it outright (Hall & Cook, 2012). Draw on the module's descriptions of differentiated instruction, learner autonomy, and feedback to show how these principles connect to everyday teaching decisions. End with an honest, encouraging note: language acquisition is complex, theories evolve, and good teachers stay curious and observant rather than dogmatic.
